\subsection{Cross-Model Generalization: LLaMA-3.2-3B Cold-Start Failure}
\label{app:llama-coldstart}

To probe cross-architecture generalization, we applied the identical GRPO configuration (Table~\ref{tab:hyperparams}) to LLaMA-3.2-3B (3B parameters; execution-only reward, seed~42, $K{=}4$ rollouts, FOLIO training set).

The model produced zero valid Prover9 output across 60 of the planned 500 training steps: reward, policy loss, and gradient norm remained at zero throughout, and training was terminated early.
Manual inspection of generations revealed natural-language text (e.g., homework-style problem restatements and conversational responses) with no first-order logic syntax.
Because $r_{\text{exec}}{=}0$ for all $K$ rollouts on every prompt, the GRPO advantage signal is identically zero and no policy update occurs.

This result establishes a \emph{capability threshold} for GRPO-based formalization: the base model must possess at minimum a rudimentary ability to generate syntactically valid solver input for the RL loop to produce any learning signal.
Qwen3-4B crosses this threshold (non-zero prove rates within the first 10 steps), while LLaMA-3.2-3B does not despite comparable parameter count (3B vs.\ 4B).
The failure likely reflects differences in pretraining data composition---specifically, exposure to formal logic and structured symbolic syntax---rather than model scale \emph{per se}.

An SFT warmstart phase (supervised fine-tuning on a small set of gold formalizations before switching to GRPO) could potentially lift models below this threshold into the regime where RL training produces signal.
This implies that the hacking phenomena reported in the main paper require models already capable of producing structurally valid output; below the capability threshold, RL produces no signal rather than degenerate signal.
